program.name: Strategic Planning Intensive
program.overview: A company's strategic plan is essential to making decisions, especially when resources are limited. You will leave this intensive with a working strategic plan that answers two fundamental questions: Where are we going, and how will we get there? You will define your mission, vision, and values; establish financial and other goals for the next three years; and identify the strategic initiatives and priorities needed to achieve them. You will also outline near-term tactics, the resources required to execute your plan, and metrics to gauge progress and effectiveness. Lastly, you will receive a customizable dashboard template designed for use with AI to help monitor progress against your strategic plan and support ongoing decision-making.
learningOutcomes: Define a clear 3-year strategic direction, including mission, vision, values, and financial and non-financial goals.
Translate that direction into focused strategic initiatives, priorities, tactics, and resource requirements to be used in aligning team and in making decisions.
Establish meaningful metrics and a dashboard approach to monitor progress and support ongoing decision-making.
Pressure-test and strengthen their strategic plan through structured peer feedback and individual advisor coaching.
Deepen their relationships with PAV community, PAV and advisors

recap.source: Summary of the Workshop 1 session on Wednesday, October 28 (from the transcript). Covers what Mina and Mona taught and the next steps. It does not include what individual founders shared about their businesses.
bigIdeas: You can't do everything. At this stage (roughly $100K to $1M in revenue) there are far more things you could do than you have time, money or people for. The plan helps you decide where to focus, and when to say no or 'not now'.
Bring a rough first draft, not a perfect one. Make the best choices you can with the information you have, then test, learn and iterate.
A strategic plan is not set in stone. Review it every quarter (an hour with your team is enough) and do a deeper dive once a year.
Involve your team where you can. More perspectives make better choices, and people who help shape the plan are more bought in to executing it.
Even large companies work with imperfect data. Every plan involves educated guesses.

planFramework.eightChapters: The plan has 8 chapters. Strategic direction: 1. Mission, Vision & Values, 2. Goals, 3. Defining Choices. Execution: 4. Strategic Initiatives, 5. Essential Priorities, 6. Measurements, 7. Tactics (next year, 2027), 8. Resources (next year, 2027).
planFramework.horizon: Three-year plan: initiatives run January 2027 through 2029, with goals for fiscal year 2029. Tactics and resources get specific for 2027.
planFramework.altitude: Every part of the plan sits at an 'altitude', from big picture (mission, vision) down to near-term detail (tactics, resources). Check you're at the right altitude for the section you're writing. If you're writing your vision and end up debating which trade show to attend, you've dropped too low.

missionVisionValues.mission: Why the company exists and how you fulfill that purpose.
missionVisionValues.vision: The future state you want to create, 5 to 10 years out. Loftier and longer-lasting than the mission.
missionVisionValues.values: The principles that guide how you operate, and a real tool when you're stuck on a hard decision (for example, a people decision or how sustainable to make a product). One company kept an orange 'values chair' in its conference room to ask 'what would our values tell us to do?'
tips: Clarity of thought matters more than polished wording.
Write the mission at a higher altitude: focus on the human, emotional or health benefit, not product features. Lumi's mission is about making people safer, not about having the brightest light.
Mission and vision should be evergreen across your whole business, not tailored to different audiences. They contain a choice about who you serve. Pick a lane and own it.

goals.what: Measurable targets that define success for fiscal year 2029: revenue, profit and year-end cash, plus other important outcomes. Quantitative is best, qualitative is OK, and they should be grounded in a three-year financial model.
tips: There's no single right growth rate. It depends on your category, business model, whether you raise capital or bootstrap, and your personal ambition for the business.
Know the assumptions behind each goal: market size, product-market fit and competition for revenue; pricing and supply chain for profit; inventory, payment terms and financing for cash.
Be clear which goal matters most right now (for example revenue vs. profitability), because it shapes every decision below it.
A goal says what outcome you want, not how you'll get there. The how comes next.

definingChoices.keyLine: If the plan does not cause you to say no, or at least 'not now', to some opportunities, you aren't making enough choices.
parts: Where we focus: where you concentrate your resources.
How we create advantage: why customers or partners choose you over the alternatives.
Capabilities: what you must be genuinely good at to execute.
tips: The three parts form a cascade. A choice in one area ripples into the others.
Splitting everything 50/50 means you've made no choices.
Choices aren't permanent. Commit, test and learn, and revisit in six months or a year.

initiativesAndPriorities.initiatives: The big, multi-year buckets (2027 to 2029) you must achieve to reach your goals. Think across five areas: sales, marketing, operations (systems, processes and team), product, and finance.
initiativesAndPriorities.priorities: What must happen for each initiative to succeed. Good priorities are concrete, and they also make clear what you won't do.
initiativesAndPriorities.lumiExample: Lumi's goal: $6M in three years. Choices: specialty wholesale first, D2C second, US focus. Sales initiative: scale US specialty wholesale while building a sustainably profitable D2C business. Priorities: add accounts in outdoor, hardware and travel through sales reps (not by hiring in-house sales managers); maximize sell-through and velocity, not just doors; improve D2C profitability with disciplined customer-acquisition economics.
initiativesAndPriorities.measurements: Measurements and dashboards are covered in Workshop 2.
initiativesAndPriorities.ordering: List your Strategic Initiatives in priority order, top to bottom, with the ones most critical to your 2029 Goals first. That makes the plan more useful for decisions and for deciding where to put resources.

recap.source: Summary of Workshop 2 on Tuesday, Nov 3 (from the deck and transcript). Covers what Mina and Mona taught and next steps, not what individual founders shared in the live cases.
pageOneTips: Label each Strategic Initiative with the strategic area it addresses (Sales/Channels, Brand/Marketing, Operations/Org, Product, Financial). It clarifies your thinking and helps readers.
Keep initiatives in priority order, most important first. The order carries meaning.

An Essential Priority is what must be true or accomplished for an initiative to succeed. It is an outcome, not a task, and it can be measured. Example: priority = 'maximize retail sell-through'; tactic (Page 2) = 'train sales reps and create retailer-support materials'.

measurements.what: How you know a strategic initiative is succeeding. Think of them as mini goals for each priority: quantitative whenever possible, time-bound, and set as targets for the end of the plan (2029).
tips: Pick the few measures that reflect your priorities. Include both performance metrics (results, like revenue, sell-through, conversion) and milestone metrics (capabilities built, like an ERP launch date or a key hire).

Example categories: Sales & Distribution (revenue growth, doors, sales per door, reorders); Marketing & Customers (traffic, conversion, ROAS, acquisition cost, repeat purchases); Products & Innovation (% sales from new products, launches, patents); Financial Health (gross margin, profit, cash, runway); Operations (inventory turns, stockouts, on-time delivery); People (key hires, retention, partnerships).

Keep tracking simple: build simple shared reporting with an owner for each measure, review most measures monthly (some quarterly) with your team, and adjust. A simple consistent review beats a complicated dashboard. Measure, learn, decide, act.
measurements.lumiExample: Lumi sales measurements included: 5,000 new doors over three years, 500,000 units sold, DTC targets (1MM site visitors, 2.5% conversion, $75 average order, more than 4x ROAS, 20K new customers), and a revenue mix of 65% US wholesale, 30% US DTC and 5% international.

tacticsAndResources.pageTwo: Page 2 is the one-year view for 2027. Page 1 is the three-year view (2027 to 2029).
tacticsAndResources.tactics: Actions that move you toward your measurements, achievable within calendar year 2027. Give every tactic an owner for accountability. There are many ways to reach the same result; choose what fits your skills, resources and situation. Each year you add a new sheet with that year's tactics.
tacticExamples: Hire sales rep groups in East and West coast territories
Launch a digital ad campaign targeting a specific audience
Interview 3 branding agencies by August and hire one by September 15
Evaluate and launch a new ERP
Build a process for vetting brand collab partners and contact 5 brands each quarter
tacticsAndResources.resources: What you need to deliver the tactics. Financial: 2027 revenue, profit and year-end cash, plus any fundraising (amount, timing, equity, loans, line of credit). Infrastructure and process: equipment, manufacturing, warehouse and distribution, website and social, software, dashboards, roles and responsibilities. Team: founder and team capacity, skills to build or bring in, new hires or role changes, contractors, agencies, advisors.

recap.tacticsClinic: A repeatable way to work through any priority: share the priority, its measurement and what you have tried (3 minutes); the group compares possible tactics and what each would need (10 minutes); then choose 1 to 2 tactics with the resources, an owner and a first step (2 minutes).
usingYourPlan: Make the hard choices now. What are you saying 'no' to?
Engage your team, be as specific as possible, and pick the approaches that fit your company.
Use the plan, don't shelve it. Check progress on tactics monthly or quarterly.
Every six months, do a reality check of the full three-year plan with your team: did you get the resources you needed, and has anything changed in your products, team, finances, market or life?
recap.dashboard: Shawn, a Path Ahead founder, demoed the REI Dashboard: a one-page view of cash, ad payback, inventory and sales by channel, rebuilt from your own data exports (Shopify, ad accounts, Amazon, bank) and run in your own Claude account with Claude Code (a paid Claude plan is needed). It is read-only and keeps your data on your computer. It will be shared after REI Legal approves it, with dummy data to try first and safety tips. Questions and feature requests go in the strategic plan thread in Slack. Tip: set it up to track the measurements from your strategic plan first.
recap.followUps: The program includes 6-month and 1-year check-ins with your advisor next year. The PAV team will reach out to set those up.

aboutPAV.summary: Path Ahead Ventures (PAV) is REI Co-op's founder-forward organization and venture capital fund for founders of color in the outdoor industry. It works with U.S.-based startups owned and led by Black, Indigenous, Latina/o/x, and Asian American and Pacific Islander founders whose companies inspire and equip people in their outdoor lives. Founders of color represent an estimated 1% of outdoor entrepreneurs, and PAV's goal is to accelerate their success, whether they are just starting out or growing an established business.
support: Community network: partners, peers, mentors, and experts who provide a trusted space for growth
Capability and infrastructure: marketing reach, supply chain, and distribution
Customer connection: ways to reach new customers and to test and build
Capital investment: a $30M fund for direct equity investments

programs.Embark: For aspiring founders with an idea or plan, helping turn early-stage ideas into viable business models. Includes equity-free grants.
programs.Navigate: For businesses ready for retail, with operational, financial, and product support for wholesale growth. Includes equity-free grants and optional, flexible equity investment.

aboutPAV.commitments: PAV has committed to invest in and partner with 300 current and aspiring founders of color and to build a network of 1,000 domain experts.
aboutPAV.note: For questions about other PAV programs, eligibility, or investment, point founders to the website or the PAV team rather than making promises.

faq.Are workshops recorded?: Yes. Recordings for Workshop 1 and Workshop 2 are available (links in each workshop's details). Pavey can also recap what was covered.
faq.What if I miss a session?: Ask Pavey for a recap, watch the recording once it is shared, and email Eman (emchan@rei.com) or DM him on Slack to let him know you missed it.
faq.What if I am running late on homework or: Email Eman (emchan@rei.com) or DM him on Slack as soon as you can. Pavey cannot grant extensions.
faq.I had trouble joining breakout rooms in: Breakout rooms didn't work for some people who joined while signed into a personal or free Microsoft Teams account. If that happens, sign out and join as a guest (for example from your web browser).

Submit your final strategic plan (Pages 1 and 2) and your presentation slide. Two ways to submit, both due by 5pm PT on Monday, Nov 9: (1) upload to the shared submission folder in Google Drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Hw3HzpGdd38siIjgacA3jdovGYqAEIuy?usp=drive_link , or (2) email them to Eman at emchan@rei.com.
